Yes, $f(t) \equiv 0$ follows. Here is the proof.

**Proof.** Suppose for contradiction that $f$ is not identically zero on $I=[t_0,t_1]$. Then there exists a point $c \in (t_0,t_1)$ with $f(c) \neq 0$. Without loss of generality, assume $f(c) > 0$ (otherwise replace $f$ by $-f$, which preserves the hypothesis since the hypothesis is linear in $f$).

Since $f$ is continuous (being $C^k$ with $k\ge 2$), there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ and a closed subinterval $[a,b] \subset (t_0,t_1)$ with $a < b$ such that $f(t) \ge \delta > 0$ for all $t \in [a,b]$, for some constant $\delta = f(c)/2$.

We now construct a test function $g \in C^k(I)$ with $g(t_0) = g(t_1) = 0$ such that $\int_{t_0}^{t_1} f(t)g(t)\,dt > 0$, contradicting the hypothesis.

Define the bump function
$$
\varphi(t) = \begin{cases}
\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{1}{1-(t-c)^2/r^2}\right) & \text{if } |t - c| < r, \\
0 & \text{if } |t - c| \ge r,
\end{cases}
$$
where $r > 0$ is chosen small enough that $[c-r, c+r] \subset [a,b] \subset (t_0,t_1)$. The function $\varphi$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}$, hence $C^k$, strictly positive on $(c-r, c+r)$, and vanishes outside $[c-r, c+r]$. In particular $\varphi(t_0) = \varphi(t_1) = 0$ since $[c-r,c+r] \subset (t_0,t_1)$.

Set $g = \varphi$. Then $g \in C^k(I)$, $g(t_0) = g(t_1) = 0$, and
$$
\int_{t_0}^{t_1} f(t) g(t)\,dt = \int_{c-r}^{c+r} f(t)\,\varphi(t)\,dt.
$$
On $(c-r, c+r) \subset [a,b]$ we have $f(t) \ge \delta > 0$ and $\varphi(t) > 0$, so the integrand $f(t)\varphi(t)$ is continuous, strictly positive on $(c-r, c+r)$, and non-negative everywhere. Therefore
$$
\int_{c-r}^{c+r} f(t)\,\varphi(t)\,dt > 0,
$$
which contradicts the hypothesis that $\int_{t_0}^{t_1} f(t)g(t)\,dt = 0$ for every admissible $g$.

Hence our assumption was false, and $f(t) \equiv 0$ on $I$. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
